summary: While the crowd marvels, Jesus tells the disciples he will be handed over; the saying stays veiled and they fear to ask.

context.title: The second prediction of the Passion
paragraphs: Luke sets this short scene straight after the healing of a boy possessed by a spirit, while the crowd is still marvelling at all Jesus was doing. [c1] It is the second of his predictions of the Passion, after Lk 9:22, with parallels in Mt 17:22-23 and Mk 9:30-32. [c2][c3]

Matthew and Mark place the saying on a journey through Galilee, but in Luke the crowd’s admiration prompts it. [c4] Some commentators think the miracle had rekindled the disciples’ hopes of an earthly kingdom. [c9] Luke’s wording names only the handing over, while Mark’s parallel also speaks of death and of rising after three days. [c5]

The saying turns on a sharp contrast: the Son of Man is given into the hands of men. [c6] The disciples do not grasp it, and in the next verse they argue over which of them is the greatest. [c7] The Cambridge Bible contrasts this incomprehension with their boldness after the Resurrection and the coming of the Spirit. [c8]

original.text: θέσθε ὑμεῖς εἰς τὰ ὦτα ὑμῶν
original.translit: thesthe hymeis eis ta ōta hymōn

translationNotes.summary: Greek says “put these words into your ears”: take them into memory and keep them there.
translationNotes.body: The Greek is concrete: put or set these words into your ears. [c10] Thayer explains the idiom as taking words into memory and holding them there. [c11] Interpreters differ over which words are meant: Meyer thinks of the crowd’s amazement, while Jamieson, Fausset and Brown point to the prediction that follows. [c12] Bengel calls the ears the first degree of understanding, which the disciples’ hearts had not yet reached. [c13]

original.gloss: is about to be handed over

translationNotes.summary: Mellei paradidosthai means “is about to be handed over”: imminent, and into the power of others.
translationNotes.body: Mellei with the infinitive marks something about to happen, so several commentators render it is about to be delivered, very soon. [c14] The verb means to give into the hands of another, and with into the hands it means into someone’s power. [c15] The Expositor’s Greek Testament renders it is about to be betrayed. [c16] Bengel sees the word balancing the disciples’ thoughts between the glory they have just seen and the coming Passion. [c17]

translationNotes.summary: A rare verb, “veiled”, used only here in the New Testament; the passive leaves unsaid who veiled it.
translationNotes.body: Parakalyptō means to cover over or conceal, and this is its only New Testament occurrence. [c18] Thayer calls the phrase concealed from them a Hebraism. [c19] The passive does not say who did the veiling, and older commentators divide: Alford and Meyer read the following clause as stating a divine purpose. [c20] Barnes and Gill, by contrast, say the disciples’ own expectation of a worldly Messiah hid the meaning from them. [c21]

translationNotes.summary: Luke, like Mark, records that the disciples were afraid to ask Jesus about the saying.
translationNotes.body: Mark’s parallel at Mk 9:32 records the same fear of asking, in almost the same words. [c22] Jamieson, Fausset and Brown suggest the disciples were afraid of laying themselves open to rebuke. [c23] The Pulpit Commentary suggests instead that the saying was so unwelcome that they may have pushed it from their minds, as people do with painful forebodings. [c24] Either way, the silence leaves the saying unexplained for now. [c25]

claims.text: The passage follows the healing of a boy possessed by a spirit (Lk 9:37-43a) and is spoken while all are marvelling at everything Jesus was doing.
Lk 9:43b-45 is the second prediction of the Passion, with parallels in Mt 17:22-23 and Mk 9:30-32.
The first prediction of the Passion in Luke is at Lk 9:22.
In Matthew and Mark the second prediction comes while Jesus travels with the Twelve in Galilee, whereas in Luke it is prompted by an external occasion, the admiration of the people.
Mark’s parallel (Mk 9:31) says that Jesus will be killed and will rise after three days, while Lk 9:44 speaks only of his being handed over into the hands of men.
The saying sets the Son of Man against the hands of men, an antithesis also found in Mt 17:22 and Mk 9:31.
In the next verse, Lk 9:46, the disciples argue about which of them is the greatest.
The Cambridge Bible contrasts the disciples’ incomprehension here with their later boldness, as proof of the change wrought in them by the Resurrection and the descent of the Holy Spirit.
Commentators suggest that the miracle had rekindled the disciples’ hopes of an earthly, messianic royalty.
Θέσθε … εἰς τὰ ὦτα literally means put or set these sayings into your ears.
Thayer explains the idiom in Lk 9:44 as taking the words into memory and holding them there.
Meyer refers “these words” to the crowd’s expressions of amazement, while Jamieson, Fausset and Brown refer them to the prediction of suffering that follows.
Bengel calls hearing with the ears the first degree of comprehension and says the disciples’ hearts were still less capable of it.
Μέλλει παραδίδοσθαι is better rendered “is about to be delivered”, that is, very soon.
Παραδίδωμι properly means to give into the hands of another, and with εἰς χεῖρας it means into someone’s power, as in Lk 9:44.
The Expositor’s Greek Testament renders μέλλει παραδίδοσθαι as “is about to be betrayed”.
Bengel says the word παραδίδοσθαι balances the disciples’ thoughts between Jesus’ glory and his Passion.
Παρακαλύπτω means to cover over, hide or conceal, and Lk 9:45 is its only New Testament occurrence.
Thayer describes “it was concealed from them” in Lk 9:45 as a Hebraism.
Alford and Meyer read the ἵνα clause of Lk 9:45 as expressing a divine purpose that the disciples should not yet perceive the saying.
Barnes and Gill hold that the saying was hidden from the disciples by their own prior belief in a worldly, conquering Messiah.
Mk 9:32 records in almost the same words that the disciples were afraid to ask Jesus.
Jamieson, Fausset and Brown suggest the disciples were afraid of laying themselves open to rebuke by asking.
The Pulpit Commentary suggests the saying was so distasteful that the disciples may have dismissed it from their minds, as people often do with painful forebodings.
In Lk 9:45 the disciples do not ask, so the saying remains unexplained to them.
